Lorck, “but children of old parents do not turn out as good as they should be.”

“Well, then it will have to go its crooked course,” said Constance, and sighed resignedly.

“It probably will,” Lorck opined. “Besides, what matters is being free of prejudice.”

“How free of prejudice?” Constance asked, pausing in her sewing for a moment.

“Not allowing oneself to be bound by the chains that people themselves have forged, but following the urge of one’s heart to feel and love freely.”

“But if there is no such thing as love? You yourself said that it was nonsense, so then that matter does not arise at all,” Constance said indifferently.

“I meant the old-fashioned notions!—No such thing as love!” All at once he spoke more quietly. “It could not have been I, Nils Lorck, who said such a thing—I, who for more than a year now have carried an infatuation that—yes, so help me God, I believe it will—end by driving me mad.”

There was something breathless about him; his voice trembled, and his fingers worked nervously with the penknife. His bearing was so different from his usual superior calm. Constance had an eerie feeling of insecurity; she did not dare look up.

If only he does not say it is I, she thought. What in the world am I to do? Ugh, such a scene.

“Oh, it will probably pass without coming to that,” she said, trying to act as though nothing were happening.

“No, it is not of that kind—it has gone much too far; it has become a passion that consumes me!”

His voice was so insistent; the sound seemed to bore into her ears.

That was the worst thing thou couldst have thought of saying, she thought; she sewed furiously and bent lower over her work. What in the world was she to answer?

“And of course you have noticed it, madam—you have known it just as well as I,” he continued.

There is no escape! she thought, and felt as though she were sinking backward.

“Known—what—I?” she stammered.

“Yes, for it is you whom I love, Constance—”

She had not noticed him make any movement, and so she could not understand how it happened that he was suddenly on his knees. She wanted to say something, but could not make her tongue obey.

“Constance,” he whispered, “let this be enough now. Struggle no longer—thou art made for love, and thou shalt come to taste the sweetness of surrendering thyself to a man who loves as boundlessly as I—”

He took her hand and brought his face close to her breast; she felt his warm breath pass over her forehead.

“No, no, no!” she cried suddenly, and in a single bound was on the floor.

“Stop this, Lorck! What is the meaning of it?” she said in a reproachful tone.

“You are sending me away, madam?” He stood pale and threatening before her.

“To speak to me like that—it is horrid of you, Lorck,” Constance whimpered, looking at him helplessly.

“I ask whether you are sending me away?”

He stamped his foot hard on the floor as he stepped closer.

Constance started.

“Do not frighten me so!” she said, with a movement as though shielding herself.

Lorck crossed his arms over his chest and stared fixedly at her.

“I love thee, Constance—it is serious, far more so than even I myself knew. I give thee myself, my life, my soul—wilt thou not accept them?”

“No, oh no,” she said, involuntarily retreating.

“Why, then, hast thou played with me, woman-creature?” he asked, stepping close to her.

“I enjoyed talking with you; never was there anything else in my thoughts!” she cried vehemently, and her voice revealed that she was close to bursting into tears.

“That is a lie!” he said brutally. “Who is it who has taken thee? I want to know whom thou lovest! Thy husband, perhaps?” He laughed scornfully.

“How can you stand there insulting me in this way?” she asked, and an expression of wounded dignity, pain, and fright appeared in her eyes. “I, who have never intentionally done you any harm.”

She went over to the window.

He followed her, seized both her wrists from behind, and forced her to turn around.

“Coquette!” he snarled.

“Let me go!” she cried angrily, wrenching her hands free. “I am no coquette, but you are a man; there is a spiritual difference of race between us—that is where it comes from.”

She went to the other side of the table; there she stood looking at him with flushed cheeks and a hostile bearing.

The thought arose in Lorck that he had judged this woman wrongly. He became confused and felt humiliated; but, accustomed as he was to being master of the situation, he wanted to try to withdraw with dignity.

“Forgive me, madam—I was too impetuous,” he said with complete calm. “I realize that I have been mistaken about you. For me it has proved fateful; the Lord alone knows to what extent. But I beg you, do not hold it against me—”

“I do not hold it against you,” she said in a low voice.

“But it will be unpleasant for you to see me after this?”

“I do not know—at this moment I cannot think calmly about the matter—” she answered.

“Do you think I ought to go?” he asked quietly.

“Yes, I think you ought to,” she said gravely.

“Well, yes, as you wish; but try to look at it sensibly—you must not imagine that I am now to be banished from you. I shall never again trouble you in the way I did this evening, madam.”

“Even so, it will surely be too painful between us henceforth,” she said.

“Well, yes—you have only to command.” He bowed and left the room with measured steps.

Out in the street he walked along swinging his walking stick and ran straight into one of his friends without noticing him until he received a blow on the shoulder and a halloo shouted into his ear.

“Oh, is that thee?” he said absently, and walked on without greeting him.

But inside, Constance sat on the sofa weeping, her head buried in a velvet cushion.

So that was how she was regarded. As a shameless coquette who spread her nets to catch men. Who it was who had taken her!—So that was the degree of respect he thought it necessary to have for her; that was how low he placed her. Whether she perhaps loved her husband!—To taunt her with that as well! No, but her husband was nevertheless the only man whose love could honor her.
